books.section: Topic 4.8 Jackson and Federal Power, A. The Second Two-Party System: The Democrats and the Whigs

stimulus.text: Published in 1832, the cartoon shows President Andrew Jackson in a crown and royal robes, holding a scepter in one hand and a scroll labeled "VETO" in the other. He stands on torn papers, including one labeled "CONSTITUTION of the UNITED STATES." The caption reads "KING ANDREW THE FIRST."
stimulus.source_note: Political cartoon "King Andrew the First," published 1832, artist unknown (Library of Congress). Public domain; image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The cartoonist's decision to show Jackson standing on the torn Constitution most directly suggests that his critics believed Jackson had

options.text: ignored the Supreme Court's ruling in Worcester v. Georgia
options.misconception: Jackson's defiance of the Court is a famous charge, so it is easy to attach it to any image of him breaking rules.

options.text: given the states too much power over federal law
options.misconception: Jackson came from a states'-rights tradition, so it is easy to assume he always sided with the states.

options.text: allowed Congress to control the Second Bank
options.misconception: The Bank fight involved Congress, so it is easy to read the cartoon as a fight about who controls the Bank.

options.text: claimed presidential power beyond the Constitution's limits

rationales.A: Jackson did refuse to enforce Worcester, but the cartoon's veto scroll and crown point to his vetoes, not to the Cherokee cases.
rationales.B: Jackson defended federal power against South Carolina's nullification, so giving states too much power is the opposite of his record.
rationales.C: Jackson fought to destroy the Bank, not to hand it to Congress, and the cartoon shows him trampling the Constitution, not Congress.
rationales.D: Torn paper labeled 'CONSTITUTION of the UNITED STATES' under a crowned president says his power broke constitutional limits.
rationales.general:
1. Read the floor. The torn paper under Jackson's feet is labeled 'CONSTITUTION of the UNITED STATES.'
2. Read the figure. A crowned president standing on the Constitution says his power went past what the document allows.
Background: his critics called his vetoes and his removal of Bank deposits the acts of a king, not a president.
Remember: in a cartoon, what lies underfoot is the thing the artist says was crushed.

figures.caption: King Andrew the First, 1832. Jackson in crown and robes, holding a veto scroll.
figures.alt: A political cartoon of President Andrew Jackson in a crown and royal robes, holding a scepter and a scroll labeled VETO, standing on torn papers including the Constitution
